title: Collection Pipeline
story: The data team needs a report: take all customer orders, filter out the cancelled ones, extract just the amounts over $50, double them for the premium tier, and collect the final totals. Instead of writing one monstrous function, you build a pipeline — a chain of simple, testable stages.
why: Pipelines turn complex multi-step data processing into a series of simple transforms — each stage does one thing, the output feeds the next, and the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.
analogy: A collection pipeline is like a car wash — the car (data) enters Stage 1 (rinse/filter), moves to Stage 2 (soap/transform), then Stage 3 (wax/double), and comes out clean at the end. Each station does one job and passes the car to the next.
try_it: Add a `tax_stage` that takes 20% tax on each amount. Insert it between filter and sum. Then add a `discount_stage` — if total > 100, subtract 10. Add a `log_stage` that prints each stage's intermediate result. Observe how easy it is to reorder stages: what happens if you tax before or after the discount?
tips: Each stage takes a Vec and returns a new Vec — inputs are NEVER modified
Name stages descriptively: `filter_cancelled`, `extract_ids`, `double_values` — you can read the pipeline like a sentence
Insert new stages by adding one line between existing stages — no rewriting required
common_mistakes: Modifying the input Vec in a stage — if a downstream stage needs the original data, it's gone
Creating one massive function instead of separate stages — hard to test, hard to debug, hard to modify
Forgetting that each stage creates a new Vec — memory grows, but for playground-sized data it's fine
